1	//! Message pool: fixed-size buffers over a caller-provided
2	//! region, handed out through an intrusive LIFO free-stack —
3	//! the allocation half of the messaging layer, decoupling
4	//! "get a message" from "send it" (see the design doc's
5	//! "Messaging layer: pools and descriptor queues").
6	//!
7	//! - One `#[repr(C)]` [`PoolHeader`] spanning two cache lines
8	//!   (immutable geometry, free-stack head), followed by
9	//!   `buf_count` buffers of `buf_size` bytes each.
10	//! - The free-stack is intrusive with zero per-buffer
11	//!   overhead: a *free* buffer's first word holds the index
12	//!   of the next free buffer; an allocated buffer carries no
13	//!   header at all (in-buffer provenance is deferred — the
14	//!   descriptor is the travel form; see the design doc's
15	//!   "Descriptor and registry design (0.7.0)").
16	//! - One owning allocator pops ([`Pool::alloc`], `&mut self`
17	//!   as the in-process single-popper token); any holder
18	//!   frees ([`BufSlot::free`], the MPSC push side). The
19	//!   [`BufSlot`] guard does not borrow the pool, so any
20	//!   number of allocated buffers may be live at once —
21	//!   the decoupling the messaging layer exists for.
22	
23	use core::marker::PhantomData;
24	use core::mem::size_of;
25	use core::ops::{Deref, DerefMut};
26	use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};
27	use zerocopy::{FromBytes, IntoBytes, KnownLayout};
28	
29	use crate::{CACHE_LINE_SIZE, CacheAligned, Error, check_type};
30	
31	/// `alloc` failed: no free buffer (or a peer-corrupted
32	/// free-stack index — validation fails toward exhaustion,
33	/// never toward handing out memory the pool doesn't own).
34	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
35	pub struct Exhausted;
36	
37	/// Layout marker written by [`Pool::init`]; rejects foreign
38	/// (including ring) regions on attach.
39	const POOL_MAGIC: u32 = 0x5A43_5031; // "ZCP1"
40	
41	/// Bumped on any change to the pool region layout.
42	const POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION: u32 = 1;
43	
44	/// Free-stack terminator: no next free buffer.
45	///
46	/// - Also why `buf_count < u32::MAX`: every valid index must
47	///   be distinguishable from the sentinel.
48	const NIL: u32 = u32::MAX;
49	
50	/// Control block at offset 0 of a pool region — two cache
51	/// lines: cold geometry, then the contended free-stack head.
52	///
53	/// - line 0: geometry, written by [`Pool::init`] with `magic`
54	///   last (`Release`), read-only thereafter. Cold: per-op
55	///   paths use the handle's snapshot.
56	/// - line 1: `first_free_idx`, CAS-contended by every freer and
57	///   the allocator — sole owner of its line.
58	/// - Every field is atomic for the same reason as the ring
59	///   [`Header`](crate::Header): a peer may be mapped at any
60	///   time, and scribbles must be garbage values, never UB.
61	#[repr(C)]
62	pub struct PoolHeader {
63	    /// Layout marker ([`POOL_MAGIC`]); stored last by init
64	    /// (`Release`), loaded first by attach (`Acquire`).
65	    magic: AtomicU32,
66	    /// Pool layout version ([`POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION`]).
67	    layout_version: AtomicU32,
68	    /// Buffer size in bytes — a [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`] multiple.
69	    buf_size: AtomicU32,
70	    /// Buffer count — nonzero, `< u32::MAX` ([`NIL`]).
71	    buf_count: AtomicU32,
72	    /// [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`] this region was built with; attach
73	    /// validates it like the rest of the geometry.
74	    cache_line_size: AtomicU32,
75	    /// Free-stack head: index of the first free buffer, or
76	    /// [`NIL`] when the pool is exhausted.
77	    first_free_idx: CacheAligned<AtomicU32>,
78	}
79	
80	const _: () = assert!(size_of::<PoolHeader>() == 2 * CACHE_LINE_SIZE);
81	
82	/// A validated view over a pool region.
83	///
84	/// - Geometry is snapshotted out of the header at
85	///   init/attach: per-op paths never re-read fields a peer
86	///   could scribble on. Free-stack links live in shared
87	///   buffer memory and are validated at every pop instead.
88	pub struct Pool<'a> {
89	    /// The region's control block.
90	    header: &'a PoolHeader,
91	    /// Base of the buffer array
92	    /// (offset `size_of::<PoolHeader>()`).
93	    bufs: *mut u8,
94	    /// Snapshot of `header.buf_size`.
95	    buf_size: u32,
96	    /// Snapshot of `header.buf_count`.
97	    buf_count: u32,
98	    _region: PhantomData<&'a [u8]>,
99	}
100	
101	// SAFETY: the handle owns the allocator role; the shared
102	// state it touches (first_free_idx, next-links) is atomic,
103	// and buffer ownership is handed off with Release/Acquire
104	// ordering — same rationale as the ring endpoints.
105	unsafe impl Send for Pool<'_> {}
106	
107	impl<'a> Pool<'a> {
108	    /// Initialize a fresh region and return the pool over it,
109	    /// with every buffer on the free-stack.
110	    ///
111	    /// - `buf_size` — bytes per buffer, a [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`]
112	    ///   multiple.
113	    /// - `buf_count` — number of buffers, nonzero and
114	    ///   `< u32::MAX`.
115	    /// - The region must be [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`]-aligned and at
116	    ///   least `size_of::<PoolHeader>() + buf_count *
117	    ///   buf_size` bytes.
118	    pub fn init(region: &'a mut [u8], buf_size: u32, buf_count: u32) -> Result<Self, Error> {
119	        validate_pool_geometry(buf_size, buf_count)?;
120	        let len = region.len();
121	        // Taken exactly once — same Stacked Borrows retag
122	        // hazard as Ring::init.
123	        let base = region.as_mut_ptr();
124	        let header = pool_header_ptr(base, len)?;
125	        if (len as u64) < pool_region_size(buf_size, buf_count) {
126	            return Err(Error::TooSmall);
127	        }
128	        // SAFETY: alignment + room for the PoolHeader checked
129	        // by pool_header_ptr; region is exclusively borrowed
130	        // for 'a; any byte pattern is a valid PoolHeader
131	        // (all-atomic fields, plain-byte padding).
132	        let header = unsafe { &*header };
133	        header
134	            .layout_version
135	            .store(POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION, Ordering::Relaxed);
136	        header.buf_size.store(buf_size, Ordering::Relaxed);
137	        header.buf_count.store(buf_count, Ordering::Relaxed);
138	        header
139	            .cache_line_size
140	            .store(CACHE_LINE_SIZE as u32, Ordering::Relaxed);
141	        // SAFETY: in bounds — len >= header + buffers.
142	        let bufs = unsafe { base.add(size_of::<PoolHeader>()) };
143	        let pool = Pool {
144	            header,
145	            bufs,
146	            buf_size,
147	            buf_count,
148	            _region: PhantomData,
149	        };
150	        // Link every buffer into the free-stack: i -> i + 1,
151	        // last -> NIL, head -> 0.
152	        for i in 0..buf_count {
153	            let next = if i + 1 == buf_count { NIL } else { i + 1 };
154	            pool.next_buf_idx(i).store(next, Ordering::Relaxed);
155	        }
156	        pool.header.first_free_idx.store(0, Ordering::Relaxed);
157	        // Published last: a peer that pre-mapped the region
158	        // must never observe the magic before the geometry it
159	        // validates (same handshake as Ring::init).
160	        pool.header.magic.store(POOL_MAGIC, Ordering::Release);
161	        Ok(pool)
162	    }
163	
164	    /// Attach to a pool region another process (or an earlier
165	    /// call) already initialized, validating its header.
166	    ///
167	    /// # Safety
168	    ///
169	    /// - `region` points to `len` bytes of memory that outlive
170	    ///   `'a`, genuinely shared and writable (e.g. a
171	    ///   `MAP_SHARED` mapping).
172	    /// - At most one attached handle acts as the pool's
173	    ///   allocator (single-popper contract); any handle may
174	    ///   free.
175	    pub unsafe fn attach(region: *mut u8, len: usize) -> Result<Self, Error> {
176	        let header = pool_header_ptr(region, len)?;
177	        // SAFETY: alignment + room for the PoolHeader checked
178	        // by pool_header_ptr; caller guarantees the memory is
179	        // live and shared.
180	        let header = unsafe { &*header };
181	        // Acquire pairs with init's Release store of magic.
182	        if header.magic.load(Ordering::Acquire) != POOL_MAGIC {
183	            return Err(Error::BadMagic);
184	        }
185	        if header.layout_version.load(Ordering::Relaxed) != POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION {
186	            return Err(Error::BadLayoutVersion);
187	        }
188	        if header.cache_line_size.load(Ordering::Relaxed) != CACHE_LINE_SIZE as u32 {
189	            return Err(Error::BadCacheLine);
190	        }
191	        // Snapshot geometry once; per-op paths never re-read.
192	        let buf_size = header.buf_size.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
193	        let buf_count = header.buf_count.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
194	        validate_pool_geometry(buf_size, buf_count)?;
195	        if (len as u64) < pool_region_size(buf_size, buf_count) {
196	            return Err(Error::TooSmall);
197	        }
198	        // SAFETY: in bounds — len >= header + buffers.
199	        let bufs = unsafe { region.add(size_of::<PoolHeader>()) };
200	        Ok(Pool {
201	            header,
202	            bufs,
203	            buf_size,
204	            buf_count,
205	            _region: PhantomData,
206	        })
207	    }
208	
209	    /// Pop the first free buffer off the free-stack as an
210	    /// owned [`BufSlot`], or [`Exhausted`].
211	    ///
212	    /// - `&mut self` is the in-process single-popper token;
213	    ///   cross-process, at most one attached handle allocates
214	    ///   (see [`Pool::attach`]). The guard does **not** borrow
215	    ///   the pool — any number of allocated buffers may be
216	    ///   live at once; per-buffer exclusivity comes from the
217	    ///   free-stack protocol (each pop yields a distinct
218	    ///   index), not the borrow checker.
219	    /// - Validated pop: the head and its next-link live in
220	    ///   peer-writable memory, so both are bounds-checked;
221	    ///   corruption degrades to `Exhausted` (mirroring the
222	    ///   ring's fail-toward-`Full` occupancy check), never to
223	    ///   an out-of-bounds buffer.
224	    /// - A racing free moves the head and the CAS retries;
225	    ///   with a single popper an in-flight head node cannot be
226	    ///   removed underneath us, so there is no ABA hazard.
227	    /// - `T` geometry is asserted on each call (a mismatch is
228	    ///   a programming error, so it panics — same doctrine as
229	    ///   `reserve_slot_with`). A zero-sized `T` is legal and still
230	    ///   consumes a whole buffer: the buffer is the
231	    ///   allocation granule.
232	    pub fn alloc<T>(&mut self) -> Result<BufSlot<'a, T>, Exhausted>
233	    where
234	        T: FromBytes + IntoBytes + KnownLayout,
235	    {
236	        check_type::<T>(self.buf_size);
237	        loop {
238	            // Acquire pairs with free's Release CAS: seeing a
239	            // head index means seeing that buffer's next-link
240	            // store (and the freer's last writes) too.
241	            let head = self.header.first_free_idx.load(Ordering::Acquire);
242	            if head == NIL {
243	                return Err(Exhausted);
244	            }
245	            if head >= self.buf_count {
246	                return Err(Exhausted);
247	            }
248	            let next = self.next_buf_idx(head).load(Ordering::Relaxed);
249	            if next != NIL && next >= self.buf_count {
250	                return Err(Exhausted);
251	            }
252	            if self
253	                .header
254	                .first_free_idx
255	                .compare_exchange(head, next, Ordering::Acquire, Ordering::Relaxed)
256	                .is_ok()
257	            {
258	                return Ok(BufSlot {
259	                    header: self.header,
260	                    buf: self.buf_ptr(head),
261	                    idx: head,
262	                    _slot: PhantomData,
263	                });
264	            }
265	        }
266	    }
267	
268	    /// [`alloc`](Pool::alloc) with an injected wait policy:
269	    /// retry until a buffer frees up or the policy gives up.
270	    ///
271	    /// - `on_exhausted` is called after each failed attempt
272	    ///   with the attempt count (0-based, saturating);
273	    ///   returning `false` gives up → `Err(Exhausted)`.
274	    /// - See [`policy`](crate::policy) for shipped policies
275	    ///   and the composition model.
276	    pub fn alloc_with<T>(
277	        &mut self,
278	        mut on_exhausted: impl FnMut(u32) -> bool,
279	    ) -> Result<BufSlot<'a, T>, Exhausted>
280	    where
281	        T: FromBytes + IntoBytes + KnownLayout,
282	    {
283	        let mut attempt = 0u32;
284	        loop {
285	            match self.alloc::<T>() {
286	                Ok(buf_slot) => return Ok(buf_slot),
287	                Err(Exhausted) => {
288	                    if !on_exhausted(attempt) {
289	                        return Err(Exhausted);
290	                    }
291	                    attempt = attempt.saturating_add(1);
292	                }
293	            }
294	        }
295	    }
296	
297	    /// Buffer size in bytes (geometry snapshot).
298	    pub fn buf_size(&self) -> u32 {
299	        self.buf_size
300	    }
301	
302	    /// Buffer count (geometry snapshot).
303	    pub fn buf_count(&self) -> u32 {
304	        self.buf_count
305	    }
306	
307	    /// A non-allocating [`PoolResolver`] view of this pool,
308	    /// for registration in a
309	    /// [`PoolRegistry`](crate::PoolRegistry).
310	    ///
311	    /// - Derived from this handle (same provenance as its own
312	    ///   pointers), so no second region borrow and no Stacked
313	    ///   Borrows retag hazard — `init`/`attach` take the
314	    ///   region pointer exactly once.
315	    /// - Any number of views may exist; none can allocate, so
316	    ///   the single-popper contract stays with this handle.
317	    pub fn resolver(&self) -> PoolResolver<'a> {
318	        PoolResolver {
319	            header: self.header,
320	            bufs: self.bufs,
321	            buf_size: self.buf_size,
322	            buf_count: self.buf_count,
323	        }
324	    }
325	
326	    /// The next-free-buffer index cell of buffer `idx` — its
327	    /// first word, the intrusive free-stack link, meaningful
328	    /// only while the buffer is free.
329	    ///
330	    /// - Returns the atomic cell, not the value; symmetric
331	    ///   with the header's `first_free_idx`.
332	    /// - Callers pass `idx < buf_count` (validated pops /
333	    ///   init's linking loop), keeping the deref in bounds.
334	    fn next_buf_idx(&self, idx: u32) -> &AtomicU32 {
335	        let p = self.buf_ptr(idx) as *const AtomicU32;
336	        // SAFETY: idx < buf_count keeps the buffer in the
337	        // region validated at init/attach; the base is
338	        // cache-line aligned and buf_size is a line multiple,
339	        // so the first word is 4-aligned; all peers access it
340	        // as an atomic.
341	        unsafe { &*p }
342	    }
343	
344	    /// Pointer to buffer `idx`; callers pass
345	    /// `idx < buf_count`.
346	    fn buf_ptr(&self, idx: u32) -> *mut u8 {
347	        // SAFETY: idx < buf_count, so the offset stays inside
348	        // the buffer array validated at init/attach.
349	        unsafe { self.bufs.add(idx as usize * self.buf_size as usize) }
350	    }
351	}
352	
353	/// A non-allocating view over a pool: resolves validated
354	/// buffer indices to owned [`BufSlot`] guards on behalf of a
355	/// [`PoolRegistry`](crate::PoolRegistry).
356	///
357	/// - Created by [`Pool::resolver`]; carries the same header
358	///   ref, buffer base, and geometry snapshot as its pool.
359	/// - Cannot allocate — the single-popper token stays with the
360	///   owning [`Pool`] handle.
361	/// - Identifies its pool by header address (see
362	///   [`PoolRegistry::into_desc`](crate::PoolRegistry::into_desc)).
363	#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
364	pub struct PoolResolver<'a> {
365	    /// The pool's control block.
366	    header: &'a PoolHeader,
367	    /// Base of the buffer array (copy of [`Pool::bufs`]).
368	    bufs: *mut u8,
369	    /// Snapshot of `header.buf_size`.
370	    buf_size: u32,
371	    /// Snapshot of `header.buf_count`.
372	    buf_count: u32,
373	}
374	
375	// SAFETY: the view is read-only over its own fields; the only
376	// shared-memory mutation reachable through it is the minted
377	// guards' free CAS, which is the free-stack's any-thread MPSC
378	// push side. Allocation (the single-popper role) is not
379	// reachable from a resolver.
380	unsafe impl Send for PoolResolver<'_> {}
381	// SAFETY: all methods take &self and touch shared state only
382	// through atomics (as above), so concurrent use from multiple
383	// threads adds no non-atomic shared access.
384	unsafe impl Sync for PoolResolver<'_> {}
385	
386	impl<'a> PoolResolver<'a> {
387	    /// The pool's header address — its identity for registry
388	    /// lookups.
389	    pub(crate) fn header_ptr(&self) -> *const PoolHeader {
390	        self.header
391	    }
392	
393	    /// Buffer count (geometry snapshot).
394	    pub(crate) fn buf_count(&self) -> u32 {
395	        self.buf_count
396	    }
397	
398	    /// Buffer size in bytes (geometry snapshot).
399	    pub(crate) fn buf_size(&self) -> u32 {
400	        self.buf_size
401	    }
402	
403	    /// Mint the owned guard for buffer `idx`.
404	    ///
405	    /// # Safety
406	    ///
407	    /// - The caller has validated `idx < buf_count` and `T`'s
408	    ///   geometry against this pool.
409	    /// - The caller holds the buffer's ownership (the index
410	    ///   came from a consumed guard via
411	    ///   [`PoolRegistry::into_desc`](crate::PoolRegistry::into_desc),
412	    ///   arrived with happens-before ordering, and is resolved
413	    ///   exactly once) — minting a second live guard for one
414	    ///   buffer aliases `&mut T`.
415	    pub(crate) unsafe fn slot_from_idx<T>(&self, idx: u32) -> BufSlot<'a, T>
416	    where
417	        T: FromBytes + IntoBytes + KnownLayout,
418	    {
419	        // SAFETY: idx < buf_count (caller contract), so the
420	        // offset stays inside the buffer array validated at
421	        // init/attach.
422	        let buf = unsafe { self.bufs.add(idx as usize * self.buf_size as usize) };
423	        BufSlot {
424	            header: self.header,
425	            buf,
426	            idx,
427	            _slot: PhantomData,
428	        }
429	    }
430	}
431	
432	/// An allocated buffer, owned until [`free`](BufSlot::free):
433	/// `DerefMut` to use it as a `T` in place.
434	///
435	/// - Does not borrow the [`Pool`] — hold any number, as long
436	///   as you like; getting a buffer implies nothing about
437	///   when (or whether) it is sent or freed.
438	/// - Dropping without `free` leaks the buffer until the pool
439	///   is re-initialized (the abandon analog of the ring's
440	///   guards, with the opposite consequence).
441	pub struct BufSlot<'p, T> {
442	    /// The pool's control block (for the free CAS).
443	    header: &'p PoolHeader,
444	    /// Base of the owned buffer. Raw, and references are
445	    /// minted per access — same aliasing rationale as the
446	    /// ring guards.
447	    buf: *mut u8,
448	    /// This buffer's index (the value free pushes).
449	    idx: u32,
450	    /// The guard acts as a `&mut T` into the region.
451	    _slot: PhantomData<&'p mut T>,
452	}
453	
454	// SAFETY: the guard owns its buffer exclusively (the pop
455	// removed it from every shared structure); free's CAS is the
456	// only shared-state touch and is properly ordered.
457	unsafe impl<T: Send> Send for BufSlot<'_, T> {}
458	
459	impl<T> Deref for BufSlot<'_, T> {
460	    type Target = T;
461	    /// Read access to the buffer as a `T`.
462	    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
463	        // SAFETY: buf is in-bounds and cache-line aligned
464	        // (validated geometry), any byte pattern is a valid T
465	        // (FromBytes bound at alloc), and the pop gave this
466	        // guard sole ownership until free.
467	        unsafe { &*(self.buf as *const T) }
468	    }
469	}
470	
471	impl<T> DerefMut for BufSlot<'_, T> {
472	    /// Write access to the buffer as a `T`.
473	    fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut T {
474	        // SAFETY: as in deref; &mut self gives exclusivity of
475	        // the minted reference.
476	        unsafe { &mut *(self.buf as *mut T) }
477	    }
478	}
479	
480	impl<T> BufSlot<'_, T> {
481	    /// The owning pool's header address — matched against a
482	    /// registry entry's [`PoolResolver::header_ptr`] by
483	    /// [`PoolRegistry::into_desc`](crate::PoolRegistry::into_desc).
484	    pub(crate) fn header_ptr(&self) -> *const PoolHeader {
485	        self.header
486	    }
487	
488	    /// This buffer's index (the descriptor payload).
489	    pub(crate) fn idx(&self) -> u32 {
490	        self.idx
491	    }
492	
493	    /// Push the buffer back onto the pool's free-stack.
494	    ///
495	    /// - Any holder may free — this is the free-stack's MPSC
496	    ///   push side; only allocation is single-popper.
497	    /// - The CAS retries only when another free (or the
498	    ///   allocator's pop) moves the head first.

content.text:
I'd keep it as `pool::v0`. Here's my reasoning.

**What a new `vN` means in this crate.** A sibling version gets added when the region layout or the protocol changes, and the old one stays alive for comparison. spsc v1 moved the seq words, v2 moved the seq into the slot, and mpsc v1 changed the seq values. Each one changes how memory is laid out or how the two sides agree.

**What this rung changes:**
- **Region layout:** unchanged, so `POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION` is still 1. A pool built by the old code and one built by the new code are byte-for-byte the same.
- **Protocol:** the free-stack protocol is untouched.
- **API:** additions only. `BufSlot`'s new field lives in the in-process guard, not in shared memory.
- **Callers:** nothing that already uses the pool changes.

A `pool::v1` would copy about 950 lines to add two accessors, and the two copies would have nothing to compare.

**If it were bumped anyway, it should be v1, not v3.** Each module family numbers its own versions: spsc is at v2, mpsc at v1, pool at v0. Matching pool to spsc's v3 would suggest the two change together, and they don't. The pool also serves the descriptor rings and cordyceps.

**When a pool v1 would make sense:**
- **MPSC segments:** the reclamation problem from our MPSC discussion. A generation tag in each buffer would let a slow producer detect that its segment was freed and reused, and that changes the pool's layout.
- **Batch alloc/free:** the "Batch alloc/free demo" Todo, if it needs a different free-stack protocol.

The plain version: the pool just gained two small accessors. The memory layout and the rules are unchanged, so it stays `v0`. A new version is for when the layout or protocol changes, and if the pool ever gets one, it would be `v1`, since the pool numbers its versions separately from spsc.

content.text:
I agree that a segment is an ordinary pool allocation, and the pool shouldn't need to know segments exist. Neither accessor in this rung is segment-specific, but they do change the pool's API, so here's what v3 needs from the pool and how it could get it without any pool change.

**What v3 needs.** A plain `alloc` already covers the allocation itself: v3 allocates as `()`, and `free` covers returning a segment. Two things are missing:
1. **The segment's bytes.** The producer has to init a v2 ring over the whole buffer. A `BufSlot<()>` only hands out a `&mut ()`, which covers zero bytes, not the buffer.
2. **An address from an index.** The consumer learns the next segment from the link, which is an index. It has to find that buffer and join the ring there.

A zero-sized `T` can't provide either one legally. A pointer taken from a `&mut ()` is only permitted to touch zero bytes, so widening it to the whole buffer is undefined behavior under Rust's aliasing rules, and Miri would flag it.

**Doing it with no pool change.** v3's `init` receives the whole region itself. So:
- **Region pointer:** v3 takes the region's base pointer once, and every address comes from that one pointer.
  - **Pool:** built over the region from that pointer.
  - **Segment addresses:** computed as base, plus the pool header's size, plus index times buffer size.
- **The index:** from the existing crate-private `BufSlot::idx()`.
- **Freeing:** the consumer builds a guard from the index with the existing crate-private `PoolResolver::slot_from_idx`, then calls the normal `free`.

Nothing in `src/pool/` changes, and this rung disappears from the ladder. The cost is that v3 knows how the pool lays out its buffers: header first, then evenly sized buffers. That layout is pinned by `POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION`, and it lives in the same crate.

**Keeping the two accessors.** The pool changes, but only by adding code, and each accessor holds its own unsafe code. v3 then doesn't need to know the pool's layout.

I lean toward doing it with no pool change, because it matches your view and removes a rung. I'd write a comment in v3 naming the layout assumption, and add a test that fails if the pool's buffer addresses ever stop matching that formula.

message.content: When an entity allocates from the pool is receives information about it's location and size and a "zero-copy" cast from T to that allocated space must be safe. Now that allocated segement may have interior T's and those should use "zero-copy" to cast to those types, thoughts only.

content.text:
That principle helps, and I think it settles the question.

**What it means for the pool.** An allocation is bytes: a location and a size. Any typed view over them is a zero-copy cast that the type system checks, whether it's the whole buffer as one `T` or `T`s inside it. zerocopy provides that check:
- **The `T` bounds:** `T: FromBytes + IntoBytes + KnownLayout` means every byte pattern is a valid `T`, so the bytes can never produce a bad value.
- **Size and alignment:** `T::mut_from_bytes` or `mut_from_prefix` check both at runtime, and return an error rather than creating a bad reference.
- **Inner `T`s:** slice to the offset, then cast. An offset that isn't aligned for `T` becomes an error, not undefined behavior.

**What the pool does today.** `BufSlot<T>` fixes one `T` when you allocate and lets you `Deref` to it. That's the "whole buffer as `T`" case, but the bytes themselves are never available, so inner `T`s at other offsets can't be reached safely. Under your principle, the bytes are the basic thing the pool hands out, and the typed view is a convenience layered on top.

**What that does to this rung:**
- **`BufSlot::as_mut_bytes` stays.** It isn't a segment-specific addition. It's the location-and-size the principle says an allocation should come with, and every zero-copy cast is built on it.
- **`PoolResolver::buf_ptr` goes.** The consumer doesn't need a raw pointer. It turns the link's index back into a guard with the existing `slot_from_idx::<()>`, calls `as_mut_bytes`, and joins the v2 ring over those bytes. No raw address leaves the pool, and the v3 "knows the pool layout" workaround isn't needed either.
- **v2's `Ring::init` and `attach` are already this pattern.** They take bytes and check alignment and size before laying the header and slots over them. Inside the ring, `reserve_slot_with::<T>` is the zero-copy cast to each slot's `T`. A segment is bytes from the pool, and a ring inside it validates its own layout.
- **Possibly `as_bytes(&self)` as well**, for read-only views, so the pair is complete.

**A bigger version of this.** An untyped `BufSlot` that holds only bytes, where every typed view is a cast (`as_mut::<T>()`, `as_mut_prefix::<T>()`), would follow the principle all the way. But it changes every pool call site, including the descriptor rings, the demo, and `tp-pool`. I'd make that a Todo entry, not part of this cycle.

**One caution.** zerocopy's cast needs `IntoBytes` for write access, and a type with atomic fields, like v2's header, may not meet the bounds for a plain safe cast. We think that's why v2's `init` does its own validated cast. So a structure with shared atomics keeps its own validation step, while plain message types use zerocopy directly.

The plain version: a pool allocation should just be "these bytes, this big", and safe zero-copy casts give you typed views of the whole thing or parts of it. `as_mut_bytes` is exactly that, so it stays. The raw-pointer accessor isn't needed: the consumer can get a segment's bytes from its index through the pool's existing guard.

message.content: We've been using zero-copy and we've been mutating allocations returned by the pool. Why do we need as-mut_bytes now and not before?

lastPrompt: We've been using zero-copy and we've been mutating allocations returned by the pool. Why do we need as-mut_bytes now and not before?

content.text:
Because until now, what we put in a pool buffer always had a size fixed at compile time. A v3 segment's size is only known at runtime.

**How the existing code gets zero-copy access.** Every use allocates as a concrete `T`, and `BufSlot<T>`'s `DerefMut` gives `&mut T` over the buffer, a checked zero-copy cast:
- **Descriptor rings and the demo:** `Msg { seq }` and similar fixed structs.
- **tp-pool's cordyceps row:** `RawBuf([u8; CACHE_LINE_SIZE])`, a byte array whose length is a constant. The `Node` is then laid over those 64 bytes.
- **Common thread:** `size_of::<T>()` is known when the code compiles, and `check_type` checks it against the pool's buffer size.

**Why v3 is different.** A segment holds a whole v2 ring, whose size is `v2::region_size(slot_size, seg_capacity)`. Both values are arguments to `v3::Ring::init`, so the byte count is only known at runtime:
- **`[u8; N]` doesn't work:** `N` must be a compile-time constant.
- **`[u8]` doesn't work:** it's unsized, and `alloc::<T>` needs a sized `T`.
- **v2's `Ring::init` takes `&mut [u8]` anyway,** not a `T`, because a ring is itself a runtime-sized layout: a header, then *capacity* slots.

So no `T` describes a segment, and the typed `Deref` path can't hand v3 the bytes. `as_mut_bytes` is the untyped version of the same zero-copy access, with its length taken from the pool's runtime buffer size.

**When it wouldn't be needed.** If v3's segment size were a compile-time constant (for example, a const generic for the segment's byte size), v3 could allocate `BufSlot<[u8; SEG_BYTES]>` and pass `as_mut_slice()` to `Ring::init`, exactly as the cordyceps row does with `RawBuf`. That would fix `M` and the slot size when v3 is compiled, and give up the runtime `seg_capacity` argument the sweep relies on to vary `M`.

The plain version: everything we stored in the pool so far had a size known at compile time, so casting the buffer to that type was enough. A v3 segment's size depends on arguments passed at runtime, so no fixed type fits it, and v3 needs the buffer as plain bytes of the buffer's actual length.

content.text:
Not a size parameter, I think. But the question points at the right design.

**Why a size parameter adds nothing.** Every buffer in a pool has the same size, `buf_size`, set at `Pool::init`. An allocation always hands out a whole buffer, so there's no size to choose. A `size` argument could only be checked against `buf_size`, and `alloc::<T>` already does that with `size_of::<T>()`. The buffer's size is already a runtime value, the pool's. What's compile-time is the *view* `alloc::<T>` puts on it.

**What your earlier principle suggests.** "Allocation gives location and size, and typed access is a safe zero-copy cast" would split `alloc` in two:
- **`alloc()` is untyped.** It returns a guard that is just the buffer: its address, its `buf_size`, its index, and `free`. No `T`.
- **Typed access is a cast on that guard, when you need it:**
  - `as_mut::<T>()` for the whole buffer as a `T`.
  - `as_mut_prefix::<T>()`, or a cast at an offset, for `T`s inside the buffer.
  - The byte slice itself, for runtime-sized layouts like a v2 ring.
- **Where the check moves.** The size and alignment check moves from `alloc` to the cast, which is where it actually matters. And one buffer could then hold several different `T`s at different offsets, which today's `BufSlot<T>` can't do.

**What today's typed `alloc::<T>` still gives you:**
- **Deref convenience:** `buf.seq = 1` works directly.
- **An early check:** a `T` that doesn't fit panics at `alloc`, not later at a cast.
- **Typed descriptors:** the registry's `into_desc::<T>` and `resolve::<T>` carry the type through.

**How it could look with both.** Untyped `alloc()` becomes the primitive, and `alloc::<T>()` stays as a thin wrapper, alloc plus cast, so existing call sites don't change. Then:
- **v3** uses `alloc()` and the byte slice.
- **Message code** keeps `alloc::<T>()`.
- **This rung's `as_mut_bytes`** is the untyped guard's byte accessor, exposed a bit early.

**Where to do it.** Restructuring the guard touches every call site from my last answer, plus the registry's typed descriptors. I'd keep this cycle to `as_mut_bytes`, the smallest step consistent with that design, and add a Todo entry: "Untyped pool allocation with zero-copy views", describing the split.

The plain version: the pool's buffer size is already fixed at runtime, so passing a size wouldn't change anything. The cleaner idea is that `alloc` hands back plain bytes, and you cast them to whatever types you need. That's a bigger reshaping, so I'd note it as a Todo and keep only the byte accessor for now.

content.text:
That changes my answer: with size classes, a size argument means something.

**How the layers could fit:**
- **A fixed-size pool, like today's `Pool`,** hands out untyped buffers of its one `buf_size`. Inside a single pool there's still no size to choose.
- **A segmented pool** holds several sub-pools of different buffer sizes. Its `alloc(size)` picks the smallest sub-pool whose buffers fit `size`, and returns that buffer's location and its *actual* size, which may be larger than asked.
- **Typed access** is sugar on top. `alloc::<T>()` becomes `alloc(size_of::<T>())` followed by a zero-copy cast, and `T`s inside a buffer are casts on its bytes.
- **Alignment** stays free: every buffer starts on a cache line, so any `T` aligned to 64 bytes or less fits.

**What's already in place.** A descriptor is `Desc { pool_id, buf_idx }`, and a `PoolRegistry<N>` holds several pools. So a sub-pool can be its own registered pool, a descriptor already names which sub-pool a buffer came from, and `free` already goes back to the pool the guard came from. Size classes grow on top of the registry without changing the descriptor.

**What it means for this cycle:**
- **`as_mut_bytes` still fits.** A size-class allocation returns bytes of the chosen class's size, which is exactly this accessor.
- **A question about v3's `init`.** The draft has `v3::Ring::init(region, slot_size, seg_capacity, seg_count)` build its own private `Pool`. With app-designed pools, "a segment is just another pool allocation" points toward v3 taking a pool (or a sub-pool) the app provides, sized for `v2::region_size(slot_size, M)`, rather than owning one:
  - **v3 owns its pool:** matches v0 through v2's `init(region, …)` shape. Simple, and the queue bound is the pool bound. But v3's segments can't share memory with anything else.
  - **v3 takes an app pool:** matches your design. Several queues can draw segments from one sub-pool, and the app decides the sizes. But the queue bound becomes "whatever the pool has left", and `init` stops looking like v0 through v2's.
- **The segmented pool itself** is its own cycle, and it would include untyped `alloc` with typed casts. I'd file it as one Todo entry, "Segmented pools: size-class sub-pools with untyped allocation", recording the layering above.

The plain version: with pools of several buffer sizes, `alloc` does need a size, to pick which sub-pool to allocate from, and typed allocation becomes a cast on top. The descriptor and registry already support several pools. The open question for v3 is whether it keeps a private pool, as the plan says, or takes segments from a pool the app sets up.

content.text:
The rung is reworked as option 2 and ready for review. Full validation passed, and clippy is clean for both crates.

**`src/pool/v0/mod.rs`**
- **Removed:** `BufSlot::as_mut_bytes` and `PoolResolver::buf_ptr`.
- **`Pool::alloc_bytes()`:** new and public. It returns `BufSlot<'a, [u8]>`, a guard over the whole buffer, all `buf_size` bytes. It's mutable through `DerefMut` like any other allocation, and it frees onto the same free-stack.
- **Shared pop:** `alloc::<T>` and `alloc_bytes` both now call one private `pop`. `alloc::<T>` still runs its compile-time type check first.
- **`BufSlot<'p, T: ?Sized>`:** the existing `Deref` to `T` is unchanged for sized types. A separate `Deref`/`DerefMut` for `[u8]` uses the guard's `buf_size` snapshot. `idx`, `header_ptr`, `free`, and `Send` now cover unsized views too.
- **Tests:**
  - `alloc_bytes_spans_the_buffer`: the bytes are the full, line-aligned buffer, and writes don't touch the neighboring buffer. A zero-copy `u64::read_from_prefix` reads back what was written, and bytes guards and typed guards draw from the same pool.
  - `alloc_bytes_holds_a_ring`: `Ring::init(&mut seg, …)` lays a v2 ring over a bytes guard and passes a message.

**`src/registry.rs`:** `into_desc<T: ?Sized>`, so a bytes guard can become a descriptor like a typed one.

**`TODO.md`**
- **Retitled** the rung to `feat: pool buffers as bytes`, with its ladder entry and reference updated.
- **Solution bullet:** now describes `alloc_bytes`.
- **Ladder details:** say why bytes are an allocation and not an accessor, and that the first design was dropped.
- **Segment-chain rung's intent:** now includes the crate-private bytes guard from an index for v3's consumer. It arrives with the code that uses it, so there's no dead code here.

message.content: So I assume current SPSC/MPSC and everyone else continues to work with the generic version but soon the generic version will invoke alloc_bytes?

content.text:
Yes, on both counts.

**Today.** Every existing caller is unchanged: the SPSC and MPSC descriptor paths, the registry, the demo, `tp-pool`, the examples, and the tests. `alloc::<T>()` still checks `T` against the buffer size and returns a `BufSlot<T>` that derefs to `T`, exactly as before. Under the hood, `alloc::<T>` and `alloc_bytes` are siblings: both call the same private `pop`, and they differ only in the view the guard carries.

**Later, with the Segmented pools Todo.** The layering flips so that bytes are the primitive:
- **The bytes call:** `alloc(size)`, the size-class version of `alloc_bytes`, picks a sub-pool and returns the buffer's bytes.
- **The typed call:** `alloc::<T>()` becomes that call with `size_of::<T>()`, followed by a checked conversion from the bytes guard to a `BufSlot<T>`, a zero-copy cast of the guard.
- **Callers:** still unchanged, since the typed call keeps its signature.

Doing the flip now would just route `alloc::<T>` through `alloc_bytes` plus a cast instead of calling `pop` directly. With a single buffer size it changes nothing, so I'd leave it for the segmented-pool cycle, where the size argument gives it a purpose.

The plain version: nobody else has to change. For now the typed and bytes versions share the same internals, and once pools have several sizes, the typed version will become a thin layer over the bytes version.

I marked the rung `(done)`, and fast validation passed. This is the proposed description:

Title: `feat: pool buffers as bytes`

```
The pool handed out buffers only as a type fixed at compile time, so
something sized at runtime, like a ring inside a segment, could not use
a buffer. A buffer can now be taken as its bytes.

* Every allocation had to name a fixed-size type.
  - Pool::alloc_bytes returns a guard over the whole buffer as bytes,
    mutable like any allocation, and typed views are zero-copy casts on
    them.
* The guard and descriptors only worked with sized types.
  - Both accept the bytes view, so a bytes allocation frees and travels
    like any other.
```
